meta.title: Urdu B1 Intermediate
meta.subtitle: 1000 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Urdu → English (see the Urdu, recall the meaning) and English → Urdu (see an English meaning, recall the Urdu). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 1000 words for an intermediate learner, aligned to B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand the main points of clear standard input on familiar matters regularly encountered in work, school, leisure, etc.' — a learner here is able to deal with most situations likely to arise while travelling, to produce simple connected text on familiar topics, and to describe experiences and events, dreams, hopes and ambitions, and briefly give reasons and explanations for opinions and plans. The words already taught by the levels below this one are left out. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Urdu, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 86 of the 1000 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — work, money and the economy, education, the news, media and technology, government, law and society, the environment and the weather, health and medicine, travel and transport, the household and its chores, relationships and the stages of life, feelings and character, religion and festivals, abstract nouns for ideas, reasons and plans, the connectors that join sentences, and the verbs of thinking, deciding, arguing and changing — and the other 914 are the commonest remaining words of Urdu, by two frequency lists averaged, one built from film and television subtitles and one from written Urdu (Wikipedia, the web and social media), each counted by the WHOLE word, every form of a noun or a verb added together. The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words you meet most often come first; because half the count is written Urdu, the news's words (government, minister, court) come earlier than a phrase book would put them. Every headword is printed in the Urdu script, right to left and without the short-vowel marks, as Urdu is written, with a romanisation beneath it, Wiktionary's own (ā ī ū for the long vowels, a tilde for nasalisation: khānā, ma͠i), which shows the vowels the script leaves out; the Urdu Alphabet deck, the first in this collection, teaches the script itself. The 730 nouns show their gender, masculine or feminine, which every adjective, postposition and past-tense verb agrees with, and their plural; the 39 verbs show their past forms, where Urdu verbs are irregular, and behind the All forms fold their key forms and their tenses. Real example sentences come with 254 of the 1000 words, three apiece for 48 of them (Tatoeba has only a few thousand Urdu sentences), with the word picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword (whether it speaks depends on an Urdu voice being installed on your device). Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, gender, forms and romanisation: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0) and the wordfreq project's Urdu list (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
